en: The Secret Essential Ritual Manual for the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper,
composed by the Consecration Ācārya of the Translation Institute at Daxingshan Temple.
Now, for the sake of sentient beings of meager merit in the final age, I shall expound this offering ritual to the Seven Stars of the North Pole.
Regarding the ritual procedure for the sequence of the *pūjā-homa*:
within a quiet chamber, construct a water-maṇḍala,
either square or circular, each measuring one cubit (*hasta*).
Mix mugwort, calamus, frankincense, camphor, and white sandalwood with clay to form a paste and smear it [over the ground].
Within the ritual precinct, place a circular incense burner and arrange the food and fruits separately.
Regarding the food to be burned: this refers to rice, grains, fruits, cakes, clarified butter, honey, and so forth;
however, one should use only the five cereals along with milk and wood, selecting them according to the person's life-constellation (*jātaka-nakṣatra*) and inspecting their suitability.

The preliminary invocation states: With the utmost sincerity, I reverently address the Seven Luminous Nārāyaṇas of the North Pole—the Honored Stars Tiganlang, Jugumen, Luktsun, Wenkur, Lienjen, Wukur, and Pujen.
For the sake of [Name], Lord of the *Dhāraṇī*,
may he be liberated from calamities and misfortunes, may his lifespan be extended so that he may live to see a hundred autumns;
now, this maṇḍala is being established.
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and descend to this place;
please accept this homa offering and protect the patron [Name].
"May one be liberated from calamities, may one's lifespan increase, and may all wishes be fulfilled according to one's heart"—recite this three times.
Next, form the mudrā:
join the palms with the fingers hollowed.
With the two thumbs,
pinch the nails of the two ring fingers;
the two middle fingers and the two little fingers are like lotus petals.
With the two index fingers slightly opened and bent, move them back and forth;
then recite the mantra of the One-Syllable Cakravartin King,
along with the mantra for summoning the Seven Stars of the Big Dipper.
The mantra of the Uṣṇīṣa is:
Namo maṃtrabhāṣitānāṃ vācāra hūṃ. The mantra for summoning the Big Dipper (Saptarṣi) is: [as above].
*Namo samantabhadranānaye hihipho ihi ina i ka ira imuḍa tra gara ra haṃ svāhā.* With these words, take wood, grains, along with ghee, honey, oil, and so forth.
Cast it into the furnace and burn it with fire.
Then, focus your attention exclusively on observing the star of your natal destiny.
If it wavers or changes color, [it portends misfortune].

Regarding the description of the light as "illuminating, piercing, and yellow-white in appearance," one should immediately make a vow that the Tathāgata perform this according to the aforementioned method for seven days and nights. One must certainly act in accordance with these matters;

if the stars do not vanish and disappear immediately, it is certain that one has not made the request. This refers to the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper, which are the essence of the sun, moon, and five planets.
In sum, the seven luminaries illuminate the eight directions; the superior luminaries preside over the celestial deities while their subordinates correspond to the human realm.
They govern good and evil and distribute calamity and fortune.
They are the sovereigns to whom the myriad stars pay homage and the ones upon whom all spiritual beings look up.
If there are those who can pay homage and make offerings to Longevity, Merit, and Nobility,
those who do not believe and show respect will find their lives do not endure for long.
Therefore, the *Lukming Shu* (Book of Destiny) says:
In this world, there is a deity named Siming who, on every Gengshen day,
ascends to report the evils and transgressions of all people to the Heavenly Emperor;
those with grave offenses have their life-span calculations reduced accordingly.
Those with minor offenses have their records removed from the registers.
Once the accounts in the registers are cleared, the one whose life was destined to end is restored.
For this reason, the Tathāgata acts for the sake of sentient beings in the final age who possess meager merit, short lifespans, and are subject to premature death.
This explains the ritual procedure for the invocation of the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper through the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-rāja* and the performance of *homa* offerings.
For those who perform these offerings,
it causes their life-span and destiny to be removed from the register of death and restored to the register of life.
If kings construct a maṇḍala within their own palaces and perform homa,
prostrations, and offerings according to the Dharma,
the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper will be pleased and provide protection.
Dwelling long in this supreme station, they constantly enjoy peace and stability.
Their consorts, ladies, and the women of the inner palace;
their princes, ministers, high officials, and the hundred functionaries—all likewise do so.
Superiors and subordinates were harmonious and reverent, and no unlawful acts were committed.
The population flourished, crops were abundant, and the land was peaceful.
There were no calamities, nor did any strange portents appear.
Epidemics and deaths shall not arise;
within the realm, enemies and bands of robbers will naturally disperse.
Therefore, this dharma is most essential and secret.
The Secret Essential Ritual Manual of the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper (Ursa Major)
